name: Ouroboros Field Adjuster's Weathershell Coat
description:
Ouroboros field adjusters spend their working hours in places that corporate offices are not — accident sites, contested claim zones, post-incident industrial floors, and occasionally the outer Shelf where clients in arrears need to be located. Their uniform coat reflects this. The outer shell is a deep charcoal weatherproof membrane bonded to a thermal mid-layer, rated for GLMZ's lake-effect winters and the ambient chemical mist that drifts in from the refinery districts. The Ouroboros serpent-circle is embossed on the left chest in a self-healing polymer print that resists abrasion and fading. Breast and inner pockets are reinforced with RFID-shielded lining to protect the claim tablets and biometric scanners adjusters carry in the field.

The coat is designed to be professional enough to enter a Tier 3 business lobby and durable enough to walk a flood-damaged Tier 1 basement without destroying itself. Adjusters describe this as the coat's defining tension — it must look like it belongs in a boardroom and survive a demolition site. Most field adjusters develop a specific relationship with their coat over the years, treating it as a work tool rather than clothing. The coat is replaced on a three-year cycle by Ouroboros, and many adjusters negotiate to keep their old ones as a condition of renewal.
cultural_context: An Ouroboros field adjuster arriving at a claim site is a complicated presence. They represent money — the possibility of a payout — and also the machinery that decides whether that payout happens. In Tier 1 and 2 communities, the coat is recognized and produces a specific social calculation: cooperate, or don't. Adjusters who work the Shelf long enough learn to read that calculation quickly.
story_hooks: A player encounters a dead field adjuster in a Shelf building collapse — their claim tablet is locked but still transmitting.
An adjuster arrives to assess a claim that, if paid out, would destabilize a local Shelf community's relationship with a corponation.
Someone is impersonating an Ouroboros adjuster to gain access to post-incident sites before legitimate investigators arrive.

physical_description.visual_profile: A structured, authoritative coat with a professional silhouette that reads as both corporate and field-hardened. The deep charcoal creates a neutral, no-nonsense presence. The embossed Ouroboros serpent on the left chest is the only decorative element—a corporate sigil that marks the wearer as an official arbiter. The coat projects competence and institutional backing without ostentation.
physical_description.fit: Tailored but not slim; cut for mobility and layering over thermal wear. The shoulders are squared, the torso fitted enough to look professional in lobbies but loose enough to move freely at accident sites. Sleeves are slightly long, designed to cover wrist augmentation ports or biometric scanners. The hem falls mid-thigh, practical for walking through debris.
physical_description.primary_material: Outer shell is a charcoal weatherproof synthetic membrane (hydrophobic, chemical-resistant polymer blend) bonded to a thermal mid-layer rated for subzero lake-effect conditions. The RFID-shielded breast and inner pockets use a stiffer ballistic weave composite.
physical_description.texture: The outer membrane is smooth but slightly textured for grip and traction—not slick. The surface has a subtle matte finish that resists glare under industrial lighting. Up close, the self-healing polymer print on the Ouroboros emblem has a faint raised quality, like a brand mark that will slowly regenerate if scratched.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep charcoal gray as the primary color, almost black in shadow but with enough tone to show weathering and wear patterns. The Ouroboros emblem in the self-healing polymer is a slightly lighter gray or silver, creating subtle contrast on the chest. No other visible branding or accent colors.
physical_description.closures: Heavy-duty magnetic snaps down the front (silent, reliable, easier to operate in gloved conditions than zippers). RFID-shielded pocket flaps with friction-fit magnetic closures. No visible zippers—all weatherproofing is seamless.
distinctive_features: Embossed Ouroboros serpent-circle on left chest in self-healing polymer—fades less than standard prints, regenerates slowly after damage
RFID-shielded interior lining in breast pockets and inner side pockets—blocks scanning of claim tablets and biometric devices
Reinforced padding at elbows and forearms—subtle but visible under close inspection, built for leaning on industrial surfaces
Thermal mid-layer bonded to outer shell—visible as subtle quilting at seams and collar
Seamless chemical-resistant construction—no exposed stitching on the outside shell
Collar is high and structured, designed to seal against neck augmentation ports or respirator adapters
Interior label is intentionally minimal—only Daybreak Appliances mark and a serial number, no size markers visible to clients
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2-3 utility uniform. The coat is mass-produced but high-quality, built for durability over luxury. The RFID shielding and thermal rating indicate corporate backing and field legitimacy. It signals institutional authority without the expense of custom tailoring or rare materials.
physical_description.cultural_context: This is the coat of a claims adjuster—a figure caught between corporate authority and the messy reality of damage assessment. Wearing it means you have money behind you, you follow procedure, and you make final judgments. In Tier 3 and Tier 5 spaces, the coat announces both opportunity (a potential payout) and threat (an official decision-maker). Adjusters develop deep attachments to worn coats; many negotiate to keep theirs after the three-year replacement cycle, treating it as a work tool with earned credibility rather than disposable uniform.
physical_description.condition_typical: When new: pristine, with sharp creases and the Ouroboros emblem perfectly intact. After 6-12 months: minor scuffs on the forearms and elbows, beginning of wear marks at magnetic snap points. After 2+ years: visible weathering—faded patches from chemical exposure, small regenerated areas on the emblem where scratches have slowly filled in, creasing at the elbows and inside seams, possible small patches from field repairs. Most adjusters keep their coats looking broken-in but maintained; pristine coats signal inexperience to clients.
